decks.title: Introduction, Classification and IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Compounds — Part 1: Why so many carbon compounds, and how to classify them
goals: Describe the vital force theory and how Wöhler’s synthesis of urea overthrew it
Explain why carbon forms a very large number of compounds
Classify organic compounds as open chain, alicyclic, aromatic or heterocyclic
State the characteristics of a homologous series and identify functional groups

slides.heading: Organic chemistry: the chemistry of carbon compounds
slides.body_md: Part 1 — where the subject came from, why it is so large, and how its compounds are grouped.

visual.alt: Table of everyday places and the organic compounds found there

slides.narration: Namaste! Organic chemistry began as the study of compounds that came from living things, such as sugar, vinegar and oils. Today it means the chemistry of carbon compounds, and it reaches your kitchen, your medicine chest, your vehicle and your clothes. In this part we ask why carbon forms so many compounds and learn to sort them into families.

slides.heading: The vital force theory and its fall
slides.body_md: Early chemists such as Berzelius believed that organic compounds could be formed only inside living organisms, under the guidance of a mysterious **vital force**. Laboratory chemistry, they said, could make only inorganic compounds. In **1828** Friedrich Wöhler prepared **urea**, a compound of animal origin, from an inorganic salt in a flask. The theory then collapsed.

nodes.label: Vital force theory: organic compounds need living organisms
Wöhler 1828: heats ammonium cyanate, an inorganic salt
Urea, a product of animal bodies, forms in the flask

visual.alt: Flow from the vital force theory through Wöhler’s experiment to the end of the theory

slides.narration: Berzelius and others believed that only living organisms could make organic compounds, guided by a vital force. In eighteen twenty eight, Friedrich Wöhler heated ammonium cyanate, an inorganic salt, and obtained urea, which until then was known only from animal bodies. One experiment was enough to show that no vital force was needed.

slides.heading: Wöhler’s synthesis of urea
slides.body_md: Ammonium cyanate and urea have the **same molecular formula**, $\ce{CH4N2O}$, but different structures: they are **isomers**. Heating rearranges the atoms. Later syntheses, such as Kolbe's ethanoic acid (1845), confirmed that laboratory chemistry can make organic compounds.

visual.alt: Ammonium cyanate rearranging into urea on heating
visual.caption: Heat converts the inorganic salt NH₄CNO into urea.

slides.narration: Ammonium cyanate is an ionic salt of inorganic origin. On gentle heating its atoms rearrange to the covalent molecule urea. Both have the same molecular formula, so they are isomers. A few years later other chemists made ethanoic acid and more organic compounds from elements, and the old belief was finished.

slides.heading: Why organic chemistry matters
slides.body_md: More compounds contain carbon than all other elements combined. The subject underlies **medicine** (analgesics, antibiotics), **agriculture** (pesticides, fertilisers such as urea), **energy** (petroleum, natural gas), **materials** (plastics, fibres, rubber), **food** (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins) and the **chemistry of life** itself (DNA, enzymes).

visual.alt: Table of fields where organic chemistry is important

slides.narration: Organic chemistry is important because carbon compounds are everywhere. Medicines such as paracetamol and penicillin, fuels such as petrol and cooking gas, plastics, fibres and rubber, urea for crops, soaps and dyes, and every food we eat are organic. Life itself, including DNA and enzymes, is carbon chemistry.

slides.heading: Why carbon forms so many compounds
slides.body_md: **Tetravalency:** carbon forms four covalent bonds. **Catenation:** carbon atoms join to each other in long chains, branched chains and rings, because the C–C bond is strong. **Multiple bonding:** carbon forms double and triple bonds with itself, oxygen and nitrogen. **Isomerism:** one molecular formula can fit many different structures. Add bonds to H, O, N, S and halogens, and the number of possible compounds is huge.

slides.narration: Carbon is special in four ways. It is tetravalent, forming four bonds. It shows catenation, joining to other carbon atoms in chains, branches and rings. It forms double and triple bonds. And the same atoms can be arranged in different ways, which is isomerism. This picture shows five different shapes made from just five carbon atoms.

slides.heading: Catenation and isomerism multiply the possibilities
slides.body_md: Every extra carbon atom in an alkane $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$ increases the number of **chain isomers**. These are structural isomers that differ only in the carbon skeleton.

visual.alt: Table of the number of chain isomers of alkanes with 4 to 10 carbon atoms

slides.narration: Look at how fast the number of isomers grows. Butane has two chain isomers, pentane three, hexane five, and an alkane with ten carbon atoms has seventy five. These are the possibilities for hydrocarbons alone. Add rings, double bonds and other elements, and it is easy to see why millions of organic compounds are known.

slides.heading: Classification of organic compounds
slides.body_md: On the basis of the carbon skeleton, compounds are **open chain (acyclic or aliphatic)** or **closed chain (cyclic)**. Cyclic compounds are **homocyclic** (carbocyclic: ring of carbon atoms only) or **heterocyclic** (at least one ring atom is N, O or S). Homocyclic compounds are **alicyclic** (resembling aliphatic compounds) or **aromatic** (benzene and its derivatives).

slides.narration: Compounds are first divided into open chain and closed chain. An open chain compound has no ring. A cyclic compound has a ring and is homocyclic if the ring has only carbon atoms, or heterocyclic if some ring atom is nitrogen, oxygen or sulphur. Homocyclic compounds are further split into alicyclic compounds and aromatic compounds such as benzene.

slides.heading: Ring compounds: alicyclic, aromatic, heterocyclic
slides.body_md: **Alicyclic** rings behave like aliphatic compounds. **Aromatic** compounds contain a benzene-type ring with alternating double bonds and special stability. A ring with N, O or S is **heterocyclic**, and it can be alicyclic (tetrahydrofuran) or aromatic (pyridine).

slides.narration: Here are four rings. Cyclohexane is an alicyclic ring of carbon atoms only. Benzene is aromatic. Pyridine is aromatic too, but one ring atom is nitrogen, so it is also heterocyclic. Tetrahydrofuran has an oxygen atom in a saturated ring, so it is heterocyclic and alicyclic. A compound can fit more than one label.

slides.heading: Homologous series
slides.body_md: A **homologous series** is a family of compounds with the **same functional group**, a **general formula**, and successive members that differ by a **$\ce{-CH2-}$ group** (14 u). Members show a gradual change in physical properties and similar chemical properties. Alkanes: $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$; alkenes: $\ce{C_nH_{2n}}$; alkynes: $\ce{C_nH_{2n-2}}$; alcohols: $\ce{C_nH_{2n+1}OH}$.

visual.alt: Table of the first five alkanes with molar masses that rise by 14 each time

slides.narration: Members of a homologous series have the same functional group and the same general formula, and each differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, a CH two unit with a mass of fourteen. Methane, ethane, propane, butane and pentane show this clearly: sixteen, thirty, forty four, fifty eight and seventy two. Their properties change gradually.

slides.heading: Worked example: using the general formula
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An alkene in a homologous series has a molar mass of $98\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ (C = 12, H = 1). Find its formula and the formula of the next member.

**Step 1.** General formula $\ce{C_nH_{2n}}$ gives $M = 12n + 2n = 14n$.

**Step 2.** $14n = 98$, so $n = 7$: the alkene is $\ce{C7H14}$ (heptene).

**Step 3.** The next member adds $\ce{CH2}$: $\ce{C8H16}$, $M = 112$.

visual.alt: Table of three consecutive alkenes and their molar masses

slides.narration: For an alkene the molar mass is fourteen times the number of carbon atoms. A molar mass of ninety eight gives seven carbon atoms, so the alkene is heptene with fourteen hydrogens. The next member adds one carbon and two hydrogens, giving a formula with eight carbons and sixteen hydrogens and a molar mass of one hundred and twelve.

slides.heading: Quick check: homologous series
slides.body_md: Use the general formula and the CH₂ difference to place a compound in a series.
slides.narration: Quick check. Subtract fourteen to move one member down a series, and add fourteen to move one member up.

slides.heading: Functional groups
slides.body_md: A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic chemical properties of a compound. Compounds with the same group form a family and react in the same way, whatever the length of the carbon chain.

slides.narration: A functional group is the part of a molecule that decides how it reacts. Ethanol has the hydroxyl group, ethanal the aldehyde group, propanone the ketone group, ethanoic acid the carboxyl group, ethanamide the amide group and chloroethane a halogen atom. Whatever the chain length, the group brings its own chemistry.

slides.heading: Common functional groups
slides.body_md: Learn the group, the class and one example. A double or triple bond between carbon atoms is also treated as a functional group.

visual.alt: Table of functional groups with the class of compound and an example

slides.narration: Here is the list to know. Hydroxyl gives alcohols and phenols. The oxygen bridge gives ethers. The aldehyde group sits at the end of a chain, while the ketone group sits inside it. Carboxylic acids, esters, acid chlorides and amides all contain a carbonyl group. Then come amines, nitriles, nitro compounds and halogen compounds, and finally the carbon to carbon double and triple bonds.

**Problem.** Vanillin, the flavour of vanilla, has the structure shown. Identify its functional groups and classify the compound.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: The vital force theory fell when Wöhler made urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828.
Tetravalency, catenation, multiple bonding and isomerism explain the huge number of carbon compounds.
Open chain and closed chain; closed chain is homocyclic (alicyclic, aromatic) or heterocyclic.
Homologous series: same functional group and general formula, successive members differ by $\ce{CH2}$ (14 u).
A functional group fixes the chemical behaviour of a family of compounds.

rows: Ring contains N, O or S

visual.alt: Summary table of four key terms from Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Wöhler’s urea ended the vital force theory. Carbon makes so many compounds because of tetravalency, catenation, multiple bonding and isomerism. Compounds are open chain or closed chain, and closed chain compounds are homocyclic or heterocyclic. A homologous series shares a functional group and differs by a CH two unit. Functional groups decide chemical behaviour.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: When asked why carbon forms many compounds, give all four reasons, not only catenation.
Write Wöhler’s reaction as NH₄CNO → NH₂CONH₂ and name the change as isomerisation.
A heterocyclic ring can be aromatic (pyridine) or alicyclic (tetrahydrofuran).
A functional group definition must mention its effect on chemical properties.

rows: Ketone group at the end of a chain
Aldehyde ends a chain; ketone is inside

Remember that heterocyclic rings can be aromatic or alicyclic. And in any definition of a functional group, say that it decides the chemical properties.

slides.heading: Why we need a systematic naming system
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **IUPAC** (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) system gives every compound one name that shows its structure.

visual.alt: Table of five common names and their IUPAC names

slides.narration: Trivial names such as acetone or acetic acid tell us nothing about structure and differ from place to place. The IUPAC system, framed by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, gives each compound one name from which the structure can be drawn, and each structure one name. That is the skill we practise in this part.

slides.heading: Word root, suffix and prefix
slides.body_md: An IUPAC name has a **word root** (carbons in the main chain), a **primary suffix** (ane, ene or yne for the bonds in the chain), a **secondary suffix** (the principal functional group) and **prefixes** (substituents, alphabetical, each with locants).

visual.alt: Table of word roots for chains of one to ten carbons

slides.narration: A name is built from parts. The word root says how many carbon atoms are in the main chain: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non and dec. Then comes the primary suffix, ane for single bonds, ene for a double bond and yne for a triple bond. A secondary suffix names the functional group, and prefixes name the branches.

slides.heading: Reading an IUPAC name
slides.body_md: **4-ethyl-2-methylheptane**: the longest chain has seven carbons (hept), all single bonds (ane), with a methyl group on C-2 and an ethyl group on C-4. Prefixes follow **alphabetical order** (e before m); locants are separated from words by hyphens.

Hept says seven carbon atoms in the longest chain, ane says single bonds only, and the prefixes name a methyl group on carbon two and an ethyl group on carbon four. Notice that ethyl is written before methyl because the prefixes follow alphabetical order, not the order of the numbers.

slides.heading: Rules for naming alkanes
slides.body_md: **1.** Choose the **longest continuous chain** as parent. **2.** Number it from the end that gives the **lowest locants** to the substituents (first point of difference). **3.** Name each substituent, using di, tri, tetra for repeats. **4.** Write prefixes in **alphabetical order**, ignoring di, tri and tetra. **5.** Join locants with commas and words with hyphens.

nodes.label: Arrange alphabetically and write the name

visual.alt: Flow chart of four steps for naming an alkane

slides.narration: Naming an alkane takes four steps. First find the longest continuous chain, which gives the parent name. Second, number it from the end that gives the lowest locants to the branches. Third, name each branch, using di or tri for repeats. Fourth, arrange the branch names alphabetically, ignoring di and tri, and write the name with commas between numbers and hyphens between numbers and words.

slides.heading: Alkyl groups as substituents
slides.body_md: An **alkyl group** is an alkane minus one hydrogen. Branched groups have common names that are still accepted, and IUPAC names that number the group from the point of attachment.

visual.alt: Table of alkyl groups with common and IUPAC names

slides.narration: An alkyl group is an alkane that has lost one hydrogen atom. Methyl and ethyl are simple. With three carbon atoms there are two groups: propyl, attached at the end, and isopropyl, attached through the middle carbon, whose systematic name is one methylethyl. The tertiary butyl group has three methyl groups on the attached carbon.

**Step 1.** Longest chain: six carbons, **hexane**.

**Step 2.** Methyl groups lie on three chain carbons. Numbering from the left gives locants 2, 3, 5; from the right 2, 4, 5. At the first point of difference 3 is lower than 4, so number from the left.

**Step 3.** Three identical groups: **trimethyl**.

**Name: 2,3,5-trimethylhexane.**

Three identical groups give trimethyl, so the name is two, three, five trimethylhexane.

slides.body_md: Choose the longest chain and the lowest locants.
slides.narration: Quick check. Find the longest chain first, then number from the end that gives the lowest locants to the branches.

slides.heading: Alkenes and alkynes
slides.body_md: The parent chain **must contain the double or triple bond**, even if a longer chain exists without it. Number from the end that gives the multiple bond the **lowest locant**. Use **ene** or **yne** and give the locant of the first carbon of the bond. If both double and triple bonds occur, the name ends in **en-yne** and the lowest set of locants decides; if there is still a tie, the double bond gets the lower number.

rows: Double bond at C-2, not C-3

visual.alt: Table of alkenes and alkynes with names and reasons

slides.narration: For alkenes and alkynes, the parent chain must contain the multiple bond. Number from the end that gives the double or triple bond the lowest number, and give the number of the first carbon of the bond. When both a double and a triple bond are present, the name ends in en yne, and the lowest set of numbers decides the direction of numbering.

slides.heading: Principal functional group and suffixes
slides.body_md: When a compound has several groups, the one of **highest priority** is the principal group: it becomes the **suffix** and takes the lowest locant. Every other group is a **prefix**. Halogen, nitro, alkoxy and alkyl groups are **always prefixes**.

visual.alt: Table of functional group priority with suffix and prefix forms

slides.narration: When a molecule carries more than one group, the group of highest priority becomes the suffix and gets the lowest number. The order runs from carboxylic acid, through sulphonic acid, ester, acid chloride, amide, nitrile, aldehyde and ketone, to alcohol and amine. All other groups are named as prefixes. Halogens, nitro groups and alkoxy groups are always prefixes.

slides.heading: Eight compounds, eight names
slides.body_md: Notice how the suffix changes with the group, and how the **chain is numbered from the end nearest the principal group**. In an aldehyde, acid, amide or nitrile the group carbon is C-1 and needs no locant.

In an aldehyde, an acid, an amide or a nitrile, the group carbon is always carbon one, so no locant is needed. Chloro and methoxy are prefixes. And in a ketone such as butan two one, the carbonyl carbon gets the lowest number possible.

slides.heading: Worked example: a compound with two groups
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name (i) $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2COOH}$ and (ii) $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH2OH}$.

**(i)** The acid group outranks the alcohol. Main chain: five carbons from the carboxyl carbon (C-1). The –OH sits on C-4, as a **hydroxy** prefix: **4-hydroxypentanoic acid**.

**(ii)** The alcohol outranks the double bond. Number so that C-1 carries –OH; the double bond is then on C-3: **but-3-en-1-ol**.

slides.heading: Alicyclic compounds
slides.body_md: Add **cyclo** before the name of the alkane with the same number of carbons in the ring. Number the ring so that the **principal group** (or a double bond) gets locant 1 or lowest, then the substituents get the lowest locants; ties are broken **alphabetically**. A single substituent on a ring needs no locant. When the ring has more carbons than the side chain it is the parent.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Name = prefixes (alphabetical, with locants) + word root + primary suffix + secondary suffix.
Parent chain: longest chain; for multiple bonds, the chain that contains them; lowest locants at the first point of difference.
The highest-priority group becomes the suffix; halogen, nitro, alkoxy and alkyl groups are prefixes only.
Rings take cyclo; the principal group or double bond is numbered first; ties go alphabetical.
Benzene derivatives: ortho, meta, para or 1,2- 1,3- 1,4-; special parents phenol, aniline, benzoic acid, toluene.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2: every name is built from prefixes, a word root and suffixes. Ask four questions. Which group is the principal group? Which chain or ring is the parent? Which numbering gives the lowest locants? Are the prefixes in alphabetical order? Rings take the cyclo prefix, and benzene derivatives use ortho, meta and para or locants.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Draw the full chain and number both ways before you decide the direction.
Write di, tri and tetra in the name but ignore them when ordering prefixes alphabetically.
The principal group, not the longest chain, can decide the parent chain.
Check a finished name by redrawing the structure from it.

notes.title: Introduction, Classification and IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Compounds — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Vital force theory and the importance of organic chemistry
sections.body_md: Berzelius and his contemporaries held that organic compounds could be made only in living organisms through a **vital force**. In **1828** Wöhler heated the inorganic salt **ammonium cyanate** and obtained **urea**: $\ce{NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2}$ (the two are isomers, both $\ce{CH4N2O}$). Kolbe's synthesis of ethanoic acid (1845) and later syntheses ended the theory. Organic chemistry is now the chemistry of carbon compounds (other than carbonates, carbon oxides and similar simple compounds, which are treated as inorganic). It is central to medicines, fuels, polymers, food, agriculture, dyes and the molecules of life.

key_terms.definition_md: Early belief that organic compounds can be formed only by living organisms, through a mysterious vital force.
Preparation of urea from ammonium cyanate, 1828, which disproved the vital force theory.

visual.alt: Table of fields where organic chemistry is important

sections.heading: 2. Why carbon forms so many compounds
sections.body_md: **Tetravalency:** carbon forms four covalent bonds. **Catenation:** carbon atoms link into long chains, branched chains and rings, because the C–C bond is strong. **Multiple bonding:** double and triple bonds (C=C, C≡C, C=O, C≡N). **Isomerism:** the same molecular formula can have many arrangements of atoms; the number of alkane isomers climbs from 2 (C₄H₁₀) and 3 (C₅H₁₂) to 75 for C₁₀H₂₂. Carbon also forms strong bonds to H, O, N, S and halogens.

key_terms.definition_md: The property of atoms of an element to link with each other to form chains and rings; very marked in carbon.
Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds.

sections.body_md: **Open chain (acyclic, aliphatic):** straight or branched chains, saturated or unsaturated. **Closed chain (cyclic):** contain a ring. **Homocyclic (carbocyclic):** ring of carbon atoms only; **alicyclic** (cyclohexane) or **aromatic** (benzene and its derivatives). **Heterocyclic:** ring contains N, O or S (pyridine is aromatic; tetrahydrofuran is alicyclic).

key_terms.definition_md: Cyclic compound that resembles aliphatic compounds in properties, such as cyclohexane.

sections.heading: 4. Homologous series and functional groups
sections.body_md: A **homologous series** has the same functional group and general formula, members differ by $\ce{CH2}$ (14 u), and physical properties vary gradually while chemical properties are similar. General formulas: alkane $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$, alkene $\ce{C_nH_{2n}}$, alkyne $\ce{C_nH_{2n-2}}$, alcohol $\ce{C_nH_{2n+1}OH}$. A **functional group** is the atom or group that determines the characteristic reactions: –OH, –O–, –CHO, >C=O, –COOH, –COOR, –COCl, –CONH₂, –NH₂, –CN, –NO₂, –X, C=C, C≡C.

key_terms.definition_md: A series of compounds with the same functional group and general formula in which each member differs from the next by a CH₂ unit.
An atom or group of atoms that determines the chemical properties of a compound.

sections.heading: 5. IUPAC naming of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes
sections.body_md: **Name = prefixes + word root + primary suffix + secondary suffix.** Roots: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non, dec. **Alkanes:** (1) longest continuous chain; (2) lowest locants at the first point of difference; (3) di, tri, tetra for repeated groups; (4) prefixes in alphabetical order (di, tri ignored; iso is counted, tert is not); (5) commas between numbers, hyphens between numbers and words. **Alkenes and alkynes:** the chain must contain the multiple bond; it gets the lowest locant; ene and yne; with both, en-yne and lowest set of locants, then the double bond lower.

sections.heading: 6. Functional groups in IUPAC names
sections.body_md: The group of **highest priority** is the suffix and gets the lowest locant: –COOH (oic acid) > –SO₃H (sulphonic acid) > –COOR (alkyl oate) > –COCl (oyl chloride) > –CONH₂ (amide) > –CN (nitrile) > –CHO (al) > >C=O (one) > –OH (ol) > –NH₂ (amine) > C=C (ene) > C≡C (yne). Other groups are prefixes (carboxy, hydroxy, oxo, amino, cyano). **Halo, nitro, alkoxy and alkyl groups are always prefixes.** In –COOH, –CHO, –CONH₂ and –CN the group carbon is C-1.

key_terms.definition_md: The group of highest priority in a molecule; it appears as the suffix of the name.
A group such as halo, nitro, alkoxy or alkyl that is never expressed as a suffix.

sections.heading: 7. Alicyclic and aromatic compounds
sections.body_md: **Alicyclic:** cyclo + alkane name; the principal group or a double bond takes locant 1 (or the lowest); substituents then get lowest locants; ties go alphabetical (1-ethyl-2-methylcyclopentane); one substituent needs no locant. **Aromatic:** monosubstituted benzenes are named substituent + benzene; retained names: toluene, phenol, aniline, benzaldehyde, benzoic acid, nitrobenzene. Two groups: ortho (1,2), meta (1,3), para (1,4); the special parent (phenol, benzoic acid, aniline) takes locant 1, otherwise alphabetical order decides.

key_terms.definition_md: Positions 1,2, 1,3 and 1,4 of two substituents on a benzene ring.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving only catenation as the reason carbon forms many compounds.
- Choosing the chain that looks longest in a drawing, not the longest continuous chain (rotate the structure).
- Numbering from the wrong end: compare locant sets at the first point of difference.
- Ordering prefixes by locant, or counting di and tri as part of the alphabetical order.
- Forgetting that halogen and nitro groups are never the suffix.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Names (1 mark each): parent chain, locants and prefixes correct and in order.
- Reasons (2 or 3 marks): one mark per distinct reason, with an example.
- Classification: state the class and the reason, naming the feature (ring atoms, benzene ring).

cards.back_md: Organic compounds can be made only by living organisms, through a vital force.

cards.back_md: Same molecular formula (CH₄N₂O), different structures.

cards.front_md: Four reasons for the large number of carbon compounds?
cards.back_md: Tetravalency, catenation, multiple bonding, isomerism.

cards.front_md: How many chain isomers has pentane (C₅H₁₂)?
cards.back_md: Three: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane.

questions.stem_md: A history-of-science class in Nagpur discusses the experiment that finally convinced chemists that organic compounds need no living organism. The experiment was:

options.text_md: burning sugar to obtain carbon dioxide and water
distilling alcohol from fermented grape juice
heating ammonium cyanate, an inorganic salt, to obtain urea
extracting indigo dye from plant leaves

questions.solution_md: Wöhler (1828) made urea, a product of animal bodies, from the inorganic salt ammonium cyanate in a flask — option (c). The others only transform or isolate substances that already came from living things (a, b, d).

questions.stem_md: A student lists four properties of carbon: (i) tetravalency, (ii) catenation, (iii) a very high electronegativity, (iv) the ability to form double and triple bonds. Which of these explain why carbon forms such a very large number of compounds?
questions.solution_md: Tetravalency, catenation and multiple bonding (with isomerism) account for the huge number of compounds. Carbon’s electronegativity is only moderate (2.5) and is not a reason — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A chemistry club in Mysuru draws every possible carbon skeleton for the formula C₆H₁₄ using only single bonds and no rings. The number of distinct skeletons they should find is:
questions.solution_md: Hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane make five chain isomers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Marble, used in the floors of the Taj Mahal, contains carbon. Which of the following carbon-containing substances is still treated as an inorganic compound?
questions.solution_md: Carbonates, carbon oxides and similar simple compounds are classed as inorganic even though they contain carbon — option (a). Urea, ethanol and methane are organic (b, c, d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The synthesis of urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828 weakened the vital force theory.

**Reason (R):** Urea was obtained in a flask from an inorganic salt without the help of any living organism.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: The tendency of carbon atoms to join one another to form long chains and rings is called ___.

questions.stem_md: In a school demonstration, a student heats 4.80 g of ammonium cyanate (molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹; the molar mass of urea is also 60 g mol⁻¹). If 85% of the salt changes to urea, what mass of urea, in g, is obtained?
questions.solution_md: Moles of $\ce{NH4CNO}$ $= 4.80 \div 60 = 0.0800\ \text{mol}$. Urea formed $= 0.0800 \times 0.85 = 0.0680\ \text{mol}$ (the change is 1 : 1). Mass $= 0.0680 \times 60 = 4.08\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: Name two fields in which organic chemistry is important, giving one organic compound or product from each field.

answer.model_answer_md: Medicine: paracetamol (analgesic) or penicillin (antibiotic). Fuels: petrol or LPG. Materials: polythene, nylon or rubber. Agriculture: urea or insecticides. Any two fields, each with a correct example.

questions.solution_md: Two fields with examples.

questions.stem_md: State the vital force theory. Write the equation for the reaction that disproved it.

answer.model_answer_md: The vital force theory held that organic compounds can be produced only by living organisms, through the influence of a vital force. It was disproved by Wöhler (1828), who heated the inorganic salt ammonium cyanate and obtained urea: $\ce{NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2}$.

questions.solution_md: Theory; Wöhler equation.

questions.stem_md: Nitrogen and oxygen also form bonds with their own atoms, yet carbon shows far more extensive catenation. Give two reasons for carbon’s behaviour.

answer.model_answer_md: Carbon is tetravalent and its C–C bond is very strong and stable, so long chains and rings do not break easily. Bonds between nitrogen atoms (N–N) and between oxygen atoms (O–O) are weak, because of lone pair repulsion, and such chains are unstable. Carbon can also form stable multiple bonds and bonds to many other elements.

questions.solution_md: Strong C–C bond; weak N–N and O–O bonds.

marking_scheme.step: Strong, stable C–C bond with four valencies
N–N and O–O bonds are weak (lone pair repulsion)

questions.stem_md: More than ten million carbon compounds are known, many more than for all the other elements put together. Explain this with three reasons and one example for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Catenation: carbon atoms link into chains, branched chains and rings, as in pentane and cyclopentane. Tetravalency with isomerism: each carbon forms four bonds, so one formula can have many structures, e.g. C₄H₁₀ has two isomers, butane and 2-methylpropane. Multiple bonding: carbon forms double and triple bonds, as in ethene and ethyne. (Strong bonds to H, O, N, S and halogens also add to the variety.)

questions.solution_md: Catenation, isomerism, multiple bonding.

questions.stem_md: A newspaper article says that "Wöhler proved that chemists can make anything that nature makes". Explain, with the reaction involved, what Wöhler actually showed, and say why ammonium cyanate and urea are called isomers.

answer.model_answer_md: Wöhler showed that urea, a compound until then known only from animal sources, can be made in the laboratory from an inorganic substance, ammonium cyanate, so a vital force is not necessary: $\ce{NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2}$ on heating. This one case removed the belief that organic and inorganic compounds belong to separate worlds. The two compounds have the same molecular formula, $\ce{CH4N2O}$, but a different arrangement of atoms (an ionic salt and a covalent amide), so they are isomers.

questions.solution_md: Showed laboratory synthesis; equation; isomers.

marking_scheme.step: What Wöhler showed (synthesis from an inorganic compound)
Same molecular formula, different structure: isomers

questions.stem_md: A forensic chemist in Pune analyses two alcohols from a sample. The first is propan-1-ol, C₃H₇OH. A second alcohol that is the very next member of the same homologous series has the formula:
questions.solution_md: The next homologue adds one CH₂ group to C₃H₇OH, giving C₄H₉OH — option (a). C₂H₅OH (c) is the previous member; the others do not keep the –OH group (b, d).

questions.stem_md: Thiophene, C₄H₄S, has a five-membered ring of four carbon atoms and one sulphur atom, with alternating double bonds, and it resembles benzene in its chemical behaviour. It is best classified as:
questions.solution_md: The ring contains sulphur, so it is heterocyclic; it behaves like benzene, so it is aromatic — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student sorts a shelf of laboratory reagents. Which pair of compounds belongs to the same homologous series?
questions.solution_md: Both alcohols have the –OH group and differ by one CH₂ — option (b). Ethanol and methoxymethane have different groups (a); ethanal and propanone are an aldehyde and a ketone (c); ethane and ethene differ in saturation (d).

questions.stem_md: Natural gas drilled off the Krishna–Godavari basin contains alkanes, and a nearby laboratory also stores an alkyne with nine carbon atoms per molecule. The molecular formula of this alkyne is:
questions.solution_md: The alkyne series is $\ce{C_nH_{2n-2}}$; for $n = 9$ this gives $\ce{C9H16}$ — option (b). $\ce{C9H20}$ is the alkane (a) and $\ce{C9H18}$ the alkene (c).

questions.stem_md: Aspirin, taken for fever, has a benzene ring carrying a –COOH group and, on the neighbouring carbon, an –OCOCH₃ group. Its two oxygen-containing functional groups are:
questions.solution_md: –COOH is a carboxylic acid; –OCOCH₃ (an acyl group joined to ring oxygen) is an ester — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Propanal and propanone have the same molecular formula, C₃H₆O. What group is present in propanal but not in propanone?

options.text_md: the aldehyde group, –CHO, at the end of the chain

questions.solution_md: Both contain a carbonyl C=O. In propanal it is part of –CHO at the chain end; in propanone it lies between two carbons — option (d).

questions.solution_md: False. They have similar chemical properties, but their physical properties (such as boiling point) change gradually with molar mass.

questions.stem_md: A ring that contains one or more atoms of nitrogen, oxygen or sulphur in addition to carbon is called a ___ ring.
questions.solution_md: **Heterocyclic.**

questions.stem_md: Match each general formula (n = number of carbon atoms) with the homologous series it represents.
questions.solution_md: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, alcohols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH (one –OH replacing one H of an alkane).

questions.stem_md: A gas chromatography sample from a petroleum refinery shows an alkane of molar mass 114 g mol⁻¹ (C = 12, H = 1). How many carbon atoms does one molecule contain?
A perfumery in Kannauj stores a straight-chain alcohol of the series $\ce{C_nH_{2n+1}OH}$ with a molar mass of $130\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16). Find $n$.
State two characteristics of a homologous series, and write the molecular formula of the alkene that is next to C₅H₁₀ in its series.

answer.model_answer_md: Members have the same functional group and the same general formula, and each differs from the next by a CH₂ group (14 u); their physical properties vary gradually and their chemical properties are similar. The next alkene is C₆H₁₂.

questions.solution_md: Two characteristics; C₆H₁₂.

questions.stem_md: A technician tags four reagent bottles with the formulas below. Write the functional group and the class of compound for each: CH₃CH₂CHO, CH₃COOCH₃, CH₃CH₂NH₂ and CH₃CH₂CN.

answer.model_answer_md: CH₃CH₂CHO: –CHO, aldehyde. CH₃COOCH₃: –COOR (–COO–), ester. CH₃CH₂NH₂: –NH₂, amine. CH₃CH₂CN: –CN, nitrile.

questions.solution_md: Four groups and classes.

questions.stem_md: In a quiz on ring systems, a team must classify four compounds: cyclohexane, benzene, pyridine and but-1-ene. For each, write whether it is open chain or closed chain, and, if closed, which further class applies.

answer.model_answer_md: Cyclohexane: closed chain, homocyclic, alicyclic. Benzene: closed chain, homocyclic, aromatic. Pyridine: closed chain, heterocyclic (nitrogen in the ring), aromatic. But-1-ene: open chain (acyclic), unsaturated.

questions.solution_md: Four classifications.

questions.stem_md: The boiling points of the first four alkanes (approximate, in K) are methane 112, ethane 185, propane 231 and butane 273. Use these data to describe the trend in a homologous series, give the molar mass difference between neighbours, and explain why the chemical behaviour of the four is similar.

answer.model_answer_md: Boiling point rises steadily as the chain lengthens (a gradual change in physical property, with larger van der Waals forces between larger molecules). Each member differs from the next by CH₂, a molar mass difference of 14 u (16, 30, 44, 58). The chemical behaviour is similar because all four are alkanes with the same functional group (C–C and C–H single bonds only).

questions.solution_md: Trend; 14 u; same group.

marking_scheme.step: Boiling point rises gradually along the series
Same functional group, so similar chemical properties

questions.stem_md: Propanoic acid and methyl ethanoate are both C₃H₆O₂ and are found in the same laboratory cupboard. Identify the functional group of each, state the class of compound, and say why one formula can represent two different classes.

answer.model_answer_md: Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, contains the carboxyl group –COOH (carboxylic acid). Methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃, contains the ester group –COOR (ester). The same atoms can be joined in different ways (isomerism), giving different functional groups with different properties.

questions.solution_md: Acid group; ester group; same formula, different arrangement.

questions.stem_md: Classify each of these as open chain, alicyclic, aromatic or heterocyclic, giving the reason: (i) CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂ in a gas cylinder, (ii) cyclopentane in a solvent bottle, (iii) a ring of five carbons and one oxygen in tetrahydropyran, an ether used in synthesis.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) But-1-ene is open chain (no ring), unsaturated. (ii) Cyclopentane is alicyclic (a homocyclic ring of carbon atoms that behaves like an aliphatic compound). (iii) Tetrahydropyran is heterocyclic (oxygen in the ring) and alicyclic (saturated ring, no benzene-type character).

questions.solution_md: Three classifications with reasons.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define a homologous series and give two of its characteristics. [2]

(b) A student places the following six compounds in groups by functional group and ring type: CH₃CH₂OH, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, benzene, cyclohexane, CH₃CHO and CH₃CH₂CHO. Form three pairs, say which two compounds in each pair are in the same class, and state, for each of the two ring compounds, whether it is alicyclic or aromatic. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which each member differs from the next by a CH₂ group. Characteristics: gradual change in physical properties; similar chemical properties; preparation by similar methods. (b) Pair 1: ethanol and propan-1-ol, both alcohols (homologues, –OH). Pair 2: ethanal and propanal, both aldehydes (–CHO). Pair 3: benzene and cyclohexane, both homocyclic rings, but cyclohexane is alicyclic and benzene is aromatic.

questions.solution_md: Definition and characteristics; pairs and ring types.

marking_scheme.step: (b) benzene and cyclohexane as ring pair

questions.stem_md:
Paracetamol, a common fever tablet, has a benzene ring carrying an –OH group and an –NHCOCH₃ group on opposite (1,4) carbons; its molecular formula is C₈H₉NO₂.

(a) Name the two functional groups present. [2]

(b) Classify the compound by its carbon skeleton (open or closed chain, and the further class), giving the reason. [1]

(c) A related compound, ethanamide, has the formula CH₃CONH₂. By how many CH₂ units, if any, do ethanamide and propanamide differ, and are they in the same homologous series? [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Phenolic –OH (a hydroxyl group on the ring) and the amide group (–NHCO–, a substituted amide). (b) Closed chain, homocyclic and aromatic, because it has a benzene ring. (c) Propanamide, CH₃CH₂CONH₂, has one more CH₂ than ethanamide. Both contain the amide group –CONH₂ and differ by one CH₂, so they are in the same homologous series (amides).

questions.solution_md: Groups; class; homologues.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the vital force theory and state how Wöhler’s experiment of 1828 led to its rejection. [2]

(b) Carbon compounds outnumber the compounds of all the other elements. State and explain three reasons, using a different example for each. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The theory held that organic compounds are formed only in living organisms under the influence of a vital force. Wöhler heated ammonium cyanate, an inorganic salt, and got urea, $\ce{NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2}$, so a compound of animal origin was made without any living system. (b) Catenation: carbon atoms bond to each other in long chains and rings (octane, cyclohexane). Multiple bonding: carbon forms double and triple bonds (ethene, ethyne). Isomerism: one formula fits many structures (C₅H₁₂: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane). Tetravalency lets each carbon bond to four atoms, which makes all this possible.

questions.solution_md: Theory and its rejection; three reasons.

questions.stem_md: A hydrocarbon blended into a lubricant has the structure CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The longest chain has six carbons (hexane). The methyl group is on C-3 when numbered from the left and C-4 from the right, so the lower locant is 3 — option (b). Wrong numbering gives (a); a shorter parent chain gives (c) and (d).

questions.stem_md: A flavour chemist studies a compound that has both a –CHO group and an –OH group on a four-carbon chain: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO. In its IUPAC name the suffix and the prefix are, respectively:
questions.solution_md: The aldehyde group has a higher priority than the alcohol, so it gives the suffix –al; –OH becomes the prefix hydroxy: 3-hydroxybutanal — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A dye intermediate in a Surat factory is a benzene ring with a –CH₃ group and a –NO₂ group on adjacent carbons. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: Adjacent carbons are ortho (1,2). Methyl comes before nitro alphabetically, so it takes locant 1: 1-methyl-2-nitrobenzene — option (d). (a) is meta and (b) is para; (c) numbers the wrong group as 1.

questions.stem_md: A student working on a petrol additive writes the structure (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. The correct IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The longest chain has six carbons. Numbering from the end nearest the first methyl gives 2,4; the other end gives 3,5, which is higher. Two methyl groups need "di" — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An unsaturated hydrocarbon in a plastics laboratory has the structure CH₃CH=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The five-carbon chain contains the double bond. Numbering from the left puts the double bond on C-2 (from the right it would be C-3), and the methyl group is then on C-4 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A research student isolates a compound of structure CH₃C≡CCH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The six-carbon chain includes the triple bond; numbering from the left gives the triple bond the locant 2 (from the right it would be 4), so the methyl group is on C-4 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A fragrance intermediate has the structure CH₃COCH₂CH₂OH, with a ketone and an alcohol group on a four-carbon chain. The correct IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: A ketone ranks above an alcohol, so the ketone gives the suffix and gets the lowest locant (2); –OH is the prefix hydroxy on C-4 — option (a). (b) uses the alcohol as the principal group.

questions.stem_md: A student chlorinates butanoic acid in a project and obtains CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)COOH. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The carboxyl carbon is C-1, so the carbon bearing chlorine is C-2: 2-chlorobutanoic acid — option (c). Locant 1 is already the acid carbon, and "1-oic" is never written.

questions.stem_md: Ethers are used as solvents in organic laboratories. The IUPAC name of CH₃OCH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
questions.solution_md: Ethers are named as alkoxyalkanes: the longer alkyl chain is the parent (propane) and the shorter one with oxygen is the alkoxy prefix (methoxy), attached at C-1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A six-membered ring has a double bond and an –OH group; the –OH is on the carbon next to a double-bonded carbon. The correct IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The alcohol is the principal group, so C-1 carries –OH and the ring is numbered towards the double bond, which then lies between C-2 and C-3 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A food-preservative chemist works with a benzene ring that carries a –COOH group and, on the carbon opposite to it, an –OH group. The IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The carboxylic acid outranks the phenol, so benzoic acid is the parent (C-1 carries –COOH) and –OH is the prefix hydroxy on the para carbon (C-4) — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** HOCH₂CH₂COOH is named 3-hydroxypropanoic acid.

**Reason (R):** In IUPAC nomenclature an alcohol group has a higher priority than a carboxylic acid group.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md:

questions.stem_md: True or false? The IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, a component of a camping-stove fuel, is 3-methylbutane.
questions.solution_md: False. Numbered from the end nearer the branch, the methyl group is on C-2: the name is 2-methylbutane.

questions.stem_md: Two substituents on carbons 1 and 3 of a benzene ring are said to be in the ___ position.
questions.solution_md: **Meta** (ortho is 1,2 and para is 1,4).

questions.stem_md: Match each IUPAC ending in a compound name with the class of compound it shows.
questions.solution_md: –oic acid is a carboxylic acid; –one a ketone; –nitrile a nitrile (–CN); –amide an acid amide (–CONH₂).

questions.stem_md: A student names the fuel component (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃ as "3-methylbutane". State the error and write the correct IUPAC name.

answer.model_answer_md: The chain was numbered from the wrong end. The longest chain has four carbons, and the methyl group must get the lowest locant, 2 and not 3. The correct name is 2-methylbutane.

questions.solution_md: Wrong end; 2-methylbutane.

marking_scheme.step: Numbered from the wrong end (lowest locant rule)

questions.stem_md: Two components of a petrol sample have the structures (i) CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ and (ii) CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃. Write their IUPAC names.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) 3-methylpentane (longest chain five carbons, methyl on the middle carbon). (ii) 2,2-dimethylbutane (longest chain four carbons, two methyl groups on C-2).

questions.solution_md: Names of the two alkanes.

questions.stem_md: A student is asked to write the condensed structural formulae of (i) 2,3-dimethylbutane and (ii) pent-1-yne.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃ (a four-carbon chain with methyl groups on C-2 and C-3). (ii) CH≡CCH₂CH₂CH₃ (five-carbon chain with the triple bond between C-1 and C-2).

questions.solution_md: Two condensed formulae.

questions.stem_md: Write the IUPAC names of (i) CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO, (ii) CH₃CH₂CH(NH₂)CH₃ and (iii) ClCH₂CH₂COOH, which a student found in three old lab notes.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) 3-hydroxybutanal (aldehyde is the principal group, C-1; –OH is a hydroxy prefix on C-3). (ii) Butan-2-amine (amine group on C-2 of a four-carbon chain). (iii) 3-chloropropanoic acid (acid carbon is C-1; chlorine on C-3).

questions.solution_md: Three names.

questions.stem_md: A student writes "2-ethyl-3-methylhexane" for CH₃CH(C₂H₅)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. Count the carbons in the longest chain of this structure, give the correct name, and say which IUPAC rule the student broke.

answer.model_answer_md: The longest chain runs through the ethyl group and has seven carbons: CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃. Numbering from the end nearer the branches gives methyl groups on C-3 and C-4: 3,4-dimethylheptane (the lowest locants 3,4 against 4,5 from the other end). The student broke the rule that the parent chain is the longest continuous chain (they chose a six-carbon chain).

questions.solution_md: 7 carbons; 3,4-dimethylheptane; longest-chain rule.

marking_scheme.step: Parent chain not the longest continuous chain

questions.stem_md: Write the IUPAC name of each ring compound used as a solvent or an intermediate: (i) a cyclopentane ring with –Cl and –CH₃ on neighbouring carbons, (ii) a cyclohexene ring with a –CH₃ group on the carbon next to the double bond, (iii) cyclohexane carrying a single –CH₂CH₃ group.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) 1-chloro-2-methylcyclopentane (chloro comes first alphabetically, so it takes locant 1). (ii) 3-methylcyclohexene (the double bond is C-1=C-2, so the methyl group is on C-3). (iii) Ethylcyclohexane (a single substituent needs no locant).

questions.solution_md: Three ring names.

questions.stem_md: Write the IUPAC (or retained) name of each benzene derivative made in a dyestuff workshop: (i) –CH₃ and –CH₃ on carbons 1 and 4, (ii) –OH and –CH₃ on neighbouring carbons, (iii) –NH₂ and –Cl on carbons 1 and 3 of the ring.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) 1,4-dimethylbenzene (p-xylene). (ii) 2-methylphenol (o-cresol), with phenol as the parent so –OH is C-1. (iii) 3-chloroaniline, with aniline as the parent so –NH₂ is C-1.

questions.solution_md: Three benzene derivatives.

questions.stem_md: A hydrocarbon from the alkane series in a lighter fuel has a vapour density of 36 (relative to hydrogen = 1; C = 12, H = 1). Find its molecular formula, and write the IUPAC names of two of its chain isomers.

answer.model_answer_md: $M = 2 \times 36 = 72$ g mol⁻¹. For $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$, $14n + 2 = 72$ so $n = 5$ and the formula is $\ce{C5H12}$. Two chain isomers: 2-methylbutane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, and 2,2-dimethylpropane, C(CH₃)₄ (the third is straight-chain pentane).

questions.solution_md: C₅H₁₂ = 72; isomers.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State any four rules used to name an open chain alkane by the IUPAC system. [2]

(b) Write the IUPAC names of (i) CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, (ii) CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ and (iii) CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂CHO. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) (1) Select the longest continuous chain as the parent. (2) Number it from the end that gives the lowest locants to the substituents (first point of difference). (3) Use di, tri, tetra for repeated groups, with a locant for each. (4) Arrange the prefixes alphabetically, ignoring di, tri, tetra. (5) Use commas between numbers and hyphens between numbers and words. (b) (i) 3,3-dimethylhexane. (ii) 2-methylbut-1-ene (chain must contain the double bond, at C-1). (iii) 3-chlorobutanal (aldehyde is C-1; chloro prefix on C-3).

questions.solution_md: Rules; three names.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Arrange the following groups in decreasing order of priority for choosing the principal functional group: –OH, –CHO, –COOH, –NH₂, >C=O. [2]

(b) Write the IUPAC names of (i) CH₃CH(OH)CH₂COOH, (ii) NCCH₂CH₂COOH and (iii) CH₃COCH₂CH₂CHO. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) –COOH > –CHO > >C=O > –OH > –NH₂. (b) (i) 3-hydroxybutanoic acid (acid is the suffix; –OH is hydroxy). (ii) 3-cyanopropanoic acid (the acid outranks the nitrile, which becomes the cyano prefix).
